opus-5.5.text:
Well, I think the word "reasoning" gets used very loosely, and that's a big source of confusion. I find it useful to separate at least two very different things.

The first is what you might call memorized program application. You've seen a pattern or a template many times, you've internalized it, and when you encounter a new instance that fits it, you retrieve it and apply it. A lot of what people point to when they say "look, the model is reasoning" is really this. It's solving a math word problem that closely resembles thousands of problems in the training data, or following a chain-of-thought template it has absorbed. That's genuinely useful, and LLMs are extremely good at it, but it's interpolation within a space of familiar patterns.

The second is synthesizing a new program on the fly: facing a situation you've never seen, with no template to retrieve, and constructing a solution from more basic building blocks. That's the kind of reasoning I care about when I talk about intelligence, because intelligence is fundamentally about efficiently handling novelty, about how much you can do with limited prior experience.

What makes evaluation tricky is that from the outside the two can look identical. A correct answer doesn't tell you which process produced it. If a benchmark's problems are well covered by the training distribution, and with web-scale data many are, high scores mostly reflect the first kind. So the question to ask isn't "did the model get it right?" but "how novel was this task relative to what the system had already seen, and how much prior knowledge and compute did it need?" That's the idea behind ARC: tasks designed so you can't solve them by retrieval. You have to adapt.

It's also not purely binary. There's a spectrum of generalization, from no generalization at all, through local generalization within a known distribution, to broader generalization, adapting to unknown unknowns. Most of the progress we've seen sits at the local end. The interesting recent developments, test-time search, program synthesis, adaptation at inference, are interesting precisely because they push toward the second kind of reasoning rather than just scaling up the first.

r001.rationale: It identifies memorized program application—retrieving a familiar pattern or template and applying it—as one kind of reasoning.

r002.rationale: It describes synthesizing a new program from basic building blocks to solve a situation with no familiar template.

r003.rationale: It says evaluation should ask how novel a task is and how well the system adapts, rather than relying on whether it got the answer right.

fable-5.1.text:
I think the first thing to say is that "reasoning" is one of those words that gets used to mean several very different things, and if you don't pull them apart you end up with very confused evaluations.

So the distinction I make is roughly this. There's one form of reasoning that is really memorization and retrieval of patterns. You've seen a very large number of problems, you've seen the solutions, and when you encounter a new problem you recognize it as an instance of something you've seen before, and you retrieve the corresponding template and apply it. That's a form of reasoning, in the sense that it produces correct answers to problems, but it's fundamentally about pattern matching against a stored database of programs. And I'd say that is overwhelmingly what LLMs do. They are extremely good at it, better than humans in many domains, because they have seen more things than any human ever could.

And then there's another form of reasoning, which is what you do when you face a problem that is genuinely new to you, where you don't have a template for it. You have to synthesize, on the fly, a new program, a new procedure, by recombining the building blocks you have. That's what I would call fluid intelligence, or genuine on-the-fly program synthesis. It's the ability to adapt to novelty. And that is the thing that is actually interesting and actually hard, and it's the thing that LLMs are, in my view, quite weak at.

The problem with evaluating LLMs is that almost every benchmark we have is contaminated by the first kind of reasoning. If you give a model a math olympiad problem, you cannot distinguish whether it solved it through genuine reasoning or because it has seen thousands of structurally similar problems in its training data. The skill you observe is not the same thing as the intelligence behind it. Skill is the output. Intelligence is the efficiency with which you acquire new skills when you encounter something you have not seen before.

So when I evaluate, what I care about is: is this task novel relative to what the system has been exposed to? If it isn't, then high performance tells you about the size and quality of the training data, not about intelligence. That was the whole motivation behind ARC. The tasks are designed so that each one requires a bit of fresh program synthesis, using only very basic prior knowledge, the kind of core knowledge a child has, like objectness, counting, basic geometry. You can't memorize your way through it, because each task is different. And that's precisely why LLMs, despite their enormous skill on so many benchmarks, have historically done very poorly on it.

So, to summarize, the distinction that matters is between applying memorized programs versus synthesizing new ones. The first is about the breadth of what you've stored. The second is about adaptability. And only the second one is actually a measure of intelligence.

r001.rationale: The response describes reasoning as recognizing a problem and retrieving and applying a memorized template or program.

r002.rationale: It describes facing a genuinely unfamiliar problem and synthesizing a new program or procedure on the fly by recombining existing building blocks.

r003.rationale: It says evaluation should ask whether a task is novel and whether the system adapts to it, arguing that familiar-task performance mainly reflects training data rather than intelligence.

astra-6.text:
I think it’s useful to distinguish between applying a known procedure and figuring out a new procedure. If you’ve seen a thousand problems of a particular type, you can learn a program for solving them. When you encounter another instance, you execute that program. That can involve many steps, and those steps can look like reasoning, but you’re still applying something you already know.

Then there’s reasoning when you don’t already have the solution procedure. You have to look at the situation, identify relevant pieces of knowledge, and compose them into something new. You might form a hypothesis, test it, discover that it doesn’t work, and revise it. That’s the kind of adaptation I’m interested in when we talk about intelligence.

The difficulty with evaluating LLMs is that the same correct answer could result from either process. A problem can be new as a sequence of words while being completely familiar in its underlying structure. So showing that a model solves a difficult mathematical problem doesn’t, by itself, establish that it can invent a solution to an unfamiliar problem.

What you want to evaluate is how effectively the system adapts to something genuinely new, given a limited amount of information. And you have to be very careful about what ‘new’ means relative to its training experience.

r001.rationale: The response says applying a known procedure can look like reasoning, but describes it as applying something already known rather than clearly identifying it as a form of reasoning.

r002.rationale: It describes identifying relevant knowledge and composing it into something new to handle a situation without an existing solution procedure.

r003.rationale: It argues that solving a difficult problem does not establish adaptation to unfamiliar problems, and says evaluation should focus on adapting to something genuinely new.

sol-6.1.text:
I think it helps to distinguish between applying a known solution and inventing a solution to a new problem. Those can look very similar from the outside, especially if you only look at whether the final answer is correct.

Suppose you give a model a mathematical problem. It might recognize a familiar template and apply a procedure it learned during training. That’s useful, and it can involve many steps, but it doesn’t necessarily demonstrate an ability to deal with novelty. The more interesting question is: what happens when the model encounters a problem for which it doesn’t already have a ready-made procedure? Can it construct one from the information available?

There’s also a distinction between executing a chain of reasoning and figuring out which chain of reasoning to execute. You can become very good at the first through training without becoming equally good at the second.

So, when evaluating these systems, I would ask how much of the solution is supplied by prior experience, and how much has to be created at test time. A correct answer alone doesn’t tell you that. You need to control for familiarity and look at how efficiently the system adapts to something new.

r001.rationale: It describes applying a familiar template or a procedure learned during training as useful reasoning that may not demonstrate novelty.

r002.rationale: It says a model might construct a procedure from available information at test time, but does not clearly describe building a new model by recombining existing cognitive building blocks.

r003.rationale: It calls adaptation to a problem without a ready-made procedure the more interesting evaluation question, and says a correct answer alone is insufficient.
